title: When the State Contracts Out Custody, Oversight Doesn't Follow
hook: Governments can delegate the job of locking someone up. What often fails to travel with the contract is the duty to open the records.
key_points: Custody is a core state power — but it is frequently exercised by private contractors on the state's behalf.
Public-records and inspection rules usually bind agencies, not the private firms they hire, so information can vanish at the contract boundary.
Children in custody are especially dependent on external oversight, since they rarely have independent ways to report abuse.
ProPublica reports that abuse inside a Tennessee businessman's juvenile prisons remained under wraps.
The fix is contractual and statutory: extend records access, independent inspection, and reporting duties to whoever holds custody.
content_html: Detaining someone is about as close to the core of state power as it gets, and yet many governments hire private operators to do it. That delegation is usually debated in terms of cost and conditions, but it also creates a quieter problem: the legal duties that make government visible do not automatically travel with the work. Public-records statutes and inspection regimes typically bind agencies, not contractors, so records about the very same detainees become harder to obtain the moment a private firm holds them. ProPublica's Paige Pfleger and Aliyya Swaby report on how abuse inside a Tennessee businessman's juvenile prisons remained under wraps.
extra_html: Juvenile facilities are where the gap bites hardest. A detained child has almost no independent route to the outside world — no unmonitored phone, no lawyer on retainer, often no family nearby — so mistreatment surfaces only if someone with authority goes looking. When the operator controls the records and the inspection schedule is thin, "no reports of abuse" and "no abuse" become indistinguishable from the outside. The remedy that follows is unglamorous and largely procedural, but it is where reform actually lives: write transparency into the contract itself, so that the operator is subject to public-records requests, unannounced independent inspection, mandatory incident reporting to a body that does not depend on the operator, and audits with published findings. The underlying principle is one worth carrying to any privatized public function. Delegating the task is a policy choice a government may legitimately make; delegating away accountability for it is not.

related.hook: Most legal systems treat young offenders differently — on the logic that a still-developing brain can change. So why are some children still tried in adult courts?

related.title: Freedom of Information
related.hook: You can't hold power to account for what you can't see. Freedom of information laws pry open the workings of government so citizens can actually check it.

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

flashcards.prompt: Why can outsourcing custody create an information gap?
flashcards.back_html: Public-records and inspection duties usually bind government agencies, not the private firms they contract with — so records about the same detainees become harder to obtain once a contractor holds them.

flashcards.prompt: Why are children in custody especially reliant on outside oversight?

choices.text: They rarely have independent means to report mistreatment or reach anyone outside the facility
Because they are held for shorter periods
Because they have no legal rights while detained

flashcards.explanation_html: Detained minors depend almost entirely on the facility itself for contact with the outside world, so abuse is unlikely to surface without inspection.

flashcards.prompt: What kind of fix does this pattern point to?

choices.text: Writing records access, independent inspection, and reporting duties into the contract and statute
Reducing the number of inspections to save money
Relying on the contractor's internal complaint line alone

flashcards.explanation_html: The gap is structural, so the remedy is structural: make transparency obligations follow the custody, whoever is holding it.
